New York school pauses plan to deploy human like AI robot teacher after backlash
NEW YORK (AP) — A school district in a rural corner of upstate New York is hitting pause on plans to deploy an AI-powered, humanoid robot in the classroom after state education officials, teachers and residents raised concerns, including the maker's ties to a company that produces hyper-realistic sex bots.
The Salamanca City Central School District's board approved the nearly $60,000 purchase from Realbotix with visions that "Sally," as the stationary robot with long brown hair has already been nicknamed, would enhance the education of high school students studying robotics and technology fields.
"Having a difficult time programming an Arduino board? Don't even know what an Arduino board is? Ask Sally, and she can explain it," Superintendent Mark Beehler said Tuesday.
"The robot also provides opportunities for students to learn how the robot is maintained, how it is updated with new approved content, and how to troubleshoot issues."
But as news spread in the small community located on the Seneca Nation of Indians reservation, parents and teachers worried about how students' personal information would be used.
Unionized teachers took aim at Realbotix's sex doll sister company, even as district officials and the company itself stressed the two manufacturers operate independently.
"A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms," said Melinda Person, president of the labor union New York State United Teachers.
For now, the robot pilot remains on hold as the district works through "enhanced student data privacy agreements" with the state education officials and continues outreach to the community, according to a statement the district posted Friday on its Facebook page.
State officials and teacher voice concerns
State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa said she remained concerned about the robot's role in the classroom even after her staff met with district officials.
"Although you confirmed that the robot would not have any role delivering classroom instruction, a recent presentation to the board characterized the robot as a 'tutoring platform,' " Rosa wrote in a letter to the district Friday.
She also echoed residents' concerns about what data privacy and security protections would be in place.
Unionized teachers, meanwhile, suggested the effort was a first step toward replacing flesh-and-bone educators. "Sally" will be able to move her arms and hands but have nonworking legs.
"Our students don't need robots," Person said. "They need real relationships with caring adults."
District officials defend robot purchase
Beehler stressed the pilot, which also includes rollout of a virtual, AI-powered teacher's assistant and at-home tutoring program, is not about replacing staff.
"There is no possible way a robot can replace a human in a school," he said Tuesday. "Even if it were possible, it would in no way be in the best interest of students. Teaching is a human-to-human process."
Beehler, who was connected to Realbotix through a former colleague, said the Las Vegas-based company was a natural fit for because its robots are already programmed with WozEd, a curriculum from Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak that the district uses.
Last year, a San Diego charter school rolled out two AI-powered robots purchased from Engineered Arts, a robotics company based in the United Kingdom, for $500,000.
Salamanca Schools, in social media posts, stressed that "Sally" won't be collecting students' personal information, recording audio or video of its interactions or sending data back to Realbotix.
The robot also has been programmed to steer clear of inappropriate topics such as sex, violence and gambling, and it won't be able to search the public internet or draw answers from unvetted generative AI services.
Instead, all information on "Sally" will be stored locally, with the life-sized robot consuming roughly the same amount of energy as a laptop, according to the district.
Robot maker responds to criticism
Realbotix added Tuesday that student authentication would be handled through the district's existing systems, and any student-linked information would remain encrypted and under the district's control.
The company also pushed back at suggestions that "Sally" was simply a repurposed sex doll, saying it was a "newly manufactured, purpose-built educational unit" with no modified or repurposed hardware.
The school's robot comes from Realbotix LLC, which focuses on healthcare, education, and other adult commercial applications.
A sister company, Intima LLC, holds an ownership stake in RealDoll, a longtime maker of sex dolls, including a line of AI-powered models billed as the "world's most advanced sex robot."
"Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover," the company said in a statement last week. "The two subsidiaries maintain their own management, personnel, payroll, facilities, manufacturing operations, product development, and market strategies."
Some residents remain wary
Beehler argued that it is crucial for isolated districts like Salamanca, which is located along the Allegheny River near the Pennsylvania state line, to find new ways to introduce cutting-edge products into classrooms.
"In most cases, our students need to travel 1-2 hours to have opportunities to see emergent technology," he said Tuesday. "One of the intents of the robot is to help level the playing field and motivate students to continue studying robotics, AI, and STEAM-related career pathways."
Some Salamanca residents, though, remain unconvinced.
Joplin Ficek, who graduated from Salamanca High School in 2024 and now works at a daycare, said she doesn't see any reason to have robots or AI take such a prominent role at her alma mater at all.
"They just need to hire more people who are willing to put in the effort for the children," Ficek said. "They need more interaction with the children than having some robot raise our kids."

sources.news_title: New York school pauses humanoid robot ‘Sally’ after state and union pushback
sources.text:
A humanoid robot named Sally was due to take a seat in a Western New York high-school classroom this autumn, silicone skin, long brown hair, and all. Instead she is on hold.
A plan that had quietly cleared the Salamanca school board back in June turned, over the following weeks, into a public fight over student privacy, screen time, and the company that built her, and the state’s top education official has now asked the district to wait.
The Salamanca City Central School District sits on the Seneca Nation reservation in the state’s rural southwest and educates roughly 1,300 students, about a third of whom identify as American Indian or Alaska Native.
It announced the pause on Friday, after a letter from New York State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa.
“The Department remains concerned about the effect that a humanoid robot may have within a high-school classroom,” Rosa wrote, adding that many parents, teachers, and stakeholders were “understandably concerned about the presence of artificial intelligence technology in classrooms.”
It is an unease that has followed AI into schools well beyond Salamanca.
Sally is the work of Realbotix, a Toronto firm that has spent the past year arguing that friendly, physical humanoid robots belong in the classroom rather than the lab.
The district paid $57,590 for the robot and an accompanying AI teacher’s assistant, a discount on the $95,000 list price, and planned to use her in high-school AI and robotics courses built around a curriculum from Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak.
Sally stays seated but moves her upper body and face, and the district says she carries no facial recognition, keeps no recordings, and runs on a closed network with no internet access.
Beyond the robot itself, the package included an AI assistant students could reach as an avatar on their laptops, offering homework help, feedback, and real-time translation in more than 100 languages.
What tipped a modest pilot into a statewide story was less the hardware than the maker’s lineage. Realbotix, formerly known as Tokens.com, acquired Simulcra in 2024, the parent company of RealDoll, which makes hyperrealistic sex dolls and companion robots.
Realbotix says the two divisions share no staff, premises, or technology, and that it is pursuing a full separation by September, but the association was enough to move the teachers’ unions.
“A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms,” said Melinda Person, president of New York State United Teachers.
Superintendent Mark Beehler has defended the project as a lesson in living with technology rather than pretending it away.
“Many schools are taking the easy solution of simply banning it,” he said, “but I have found that students will find a way around most rules that schools put in place.”
He has stressed that Realbotix would not have access to personally identifiable student information, and that Sally was never meant to replace a teacher, only to sit alongside one.
In Salamanca itself, opinion had split, with some parents welcoming early exposure to AI as a route to future work and others asking why the district was buying a robot rather than hiring more teachers.
The department was not persuaded, at least not yet, and the concerns it raised were the ones that now shadow almost any classroom technology: data protection, screen time, and whether the tools are ready for children at all.
Half of American parents already worry their children lean on AI too much, and researchers have separately flagged the risk to students from general-purpose AI slipping into schoolwork.
Salamanca said it would use the pause to work through enhanced student data privacy agreements and keep talking to parents before deciding what comes next.
For now, Sally waits. Realbotix chief executive Andrew Kiguel struck a conciliatory note, saying the company wanted the programme to be “demonstrably safe, fully district-approved, and strongly supported by teachers.”
Whether Salamanca’s classrooms get their robot this autumn, or at all, is no longer the district’s to settle on its own.

sources.news_title: Aborted plan for life-like robot in NY classroom alarms state teachers union
sources.text:
An aborted plan to use a life-like robotic teacher’s assistant in a Western New York school district has prompted the state teacher’s union to call for new limits on artificial intelligence in schools.
Sally, a brunette, silicone-skinned android powered by AI, was set to debut this fall in Salamanca’s high school. The town has a population of around 6,000 people and is part of the Allegany Indian Reservation, less than three hours from Cleveland. The robot was to have been manufactured by Realbotix, which has a sibling company that produces sex dolls.
But after a public outcry and concern from State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa, the Salamanca school district put the plan on pause.
Melinda Person, president of the New York State Teachers Union, argued there were still lessons to be learned from the futuristic episode. She sent an open letter to top education officials Monday pressing for “clear, enforceable statewide guardrails” on AI, including “heightened protections” against humanoid robots in the classroom.
“A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms,” Person added.
The manufacturer of the robot in 2024 shed its previous name, Tokens.com, while reportedly purchasing Simulacra, which is known for realistic sex dolls, for $16.7 million. CEO Andrew Kiguel has said Realbotix is solely focused on humanoid systems for “education, healthcare, hospitality, entertainment, customer service and wellness.”
In a press release, Realbotix wrote last month that the robot would have “natural conversation, facial expressions and realtime interaction to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences. The robot aims to encourage student participation and provide early exposure to emerging technologies.”
Kiguel said in a statement Monday that the company respects the school district’s decision to pause the rollout of the robot. “Realbotix understands the questions being raised by parents and believes they deserve clear, verifiable answers,” he said.
The robot does not record audio or video and does not use facial recognition, he said. The company pledged to not store any student data.
Kiguel also emphasized that the effort to introduce the robot into the classroom is wholly separate from any “adult-products business.”
J.P. O’Hare, a spokesperson for the New York State Education Department, said safe deployment of technology in classrooms is a top priority, and the department is developing “comprehensive statewide guidance to support the responsible use of digital tools, artificial intelligence, and emerging technologies in schools.”
The uproar over Sally embodies the growing anxiety about artificial intelligence and technology in the classroom. In New York City, Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has paused all purchases of educational software while the education department revises its AI policies. Some parents and teachers have called for a moratorium on AI in schools and stricter limits on screens in general.
On Friday, Rosa, New York’s top education official, wrote to the Salamanca superintendent that the state education department “remains concerned about the effect that a humanoid robot may have within a high school classroom,” and said officials would be monitoring the situation for legal, instructional, safety and privacy concerns, as well as any other “unforeseen consequences.”
The plan for the robot was first reported by New York Focus. Students in the rural Salamanca High School helped design the robot, selecting a youthful female figure with fair skin and long brown hair, according to the report.
“We now have a powerful solution that will not replace student learning or our valued educators but instead serves as an additional custom resource to enhance learning outcomes and increase the efficiency of educators’ planning and lesson development,” Dr. Mark Beehler, Superintendent of Salamanca City Central School District, said in the press release last month.
The price tag for the robot and related software that allows students to interact with Sally’s avatar on their laptops came to nearly $58,000.

sources.news_title: Parents and a Sex Doll Company’s Robot Teacher Collide in a New York Classroom
sources.text:
A small school district in Western New York was days away from making history for all the wrong reasons. The Salamanca City Central School District, a rural district located on Seneca Nation territory, had approved nearly $58,000 to place a lifelike humanoid robot named Sally in its high school classrooms this fall. The vendor? Realbotix, the corporate parent of RealDoll, the Las Vegas outfit famous for manufacturing hyperrealistic sex dolls.
You read that correctly. A public school district looked at a company whose flagship consumer product line exists for purposes that cannot be described in a family publication and concluded this was the right partner to sit a silicone-skinned, long-haired female android in front of eleventh and twelfth graders.
Mercifully, the plan is now on hold. On July 24, hours after New York State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa sent the district a letter warning that “the Department remains concerned about the effect that a humanoid robot may have” in a high school classroom, Salamanca announced on Facebook that the pilot was paused while officials work through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the state and continue engaging with the community.
How Did This Happen in the First Place?
The district’s school board approved the $57,590 purchase at a meeting last month. The package included the robot itself and an AI avatar program allowing students to interact with a digital version of Sally on their laptops, submitting homework photos for feedback and receiving translations in over 100 languages. Sally would remain seated but was designed with silicone skin, a wide range of facial expressions, and upper-body gestures, teaching coding, robotics, and artificial intelligence courses.
Superintendent Mark Beehler defended the move as forward-thinking, telling Syracuse.com that banning AI is the easy way out and that “students will find a way around most rules” schools put in place. That much is true. It is also entirely beside the point. Teaching students to use AI responsibly does not require purchasing a humanoid android from a company with Realbotix’s pedigree.
And what a pedigree it is. Realbotix was formerly known as Tokens.com, a Toronto crypto company best known for spending millions on imaginary “land” in the metaverse. When that fad collapsed, it pivoted by acquiring Simulacra, the parent company of RealDoll, in 2024.
RealDoll’s subsidiary showed off the first male sex robot, complete with robotic anatomy, back in 2022. The company now insists its education division shares no employees, payroll, facilities, or technology with the adult side of the house, and a spokesperson says an ownership-level separation through a Nasdaq-listed company is expected by September. Perhaps. But a corporate reorganization announced under public pressure is not the same thing as a clean history.
The Backlash Was Swift and Bipartisan
Credit where due. This was not a partisan revolt but a parental one. When the district posted its board meeting online, the comments filled with parents asking the obvious question, with one summarizing the sentiment bluntly by asking why the district could not simply hire another teacher. The New York State United Teachers union, hardly a bastion of conservatism, issued a statement declaring that a robot built by a company associated with sex dolls “has no business in our classrooms.”
When conservative Christian parents and the state teachers union arrive at the same conclusion, the conclusion is probably correct.
The district, for its part, had promised the robot “will never replace teachers, staff members, or meaningful human interaction.” Realbotix CEO Andrew Kiguel struck a conciliatory tone after the pause, saying the company wants the program to be “demonstrably safe, fully district-approved, and strongly supported by teachers.” Notice what nobody disputes, though.
Kiguel has said openly that his company’s ambition is to build machines indistinguishable from humans. That is precisely the problem. Children are formed by relationships with real people, real teachers, real accountability. A machine engineered to simulate humanity, built by a firm that made its fortune simulating intimacy, is not a teaching aid. It is a category error with a price tag.
The Deeper Sickness
Strip away the tabloid absurdity and a serious question remains. Why is our culture so eager to hand children to machines? The same civilization that discovered smartphones and social media hollowed out a generation’s mental health is now beta-testing silicone androids on teenagers in a district that could have used that $58,000 on books, tutors, or a stipend to attract a human being to the front of the classroom.
Scripture saw this impulse coming three thousand years ago. “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men’s hands. They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.”
The psalmist was describing idols with mouths that speak not and eyes that see not. We have improved on the ancients only in one respect. Our idols talk back.
Salamanca’s parents deserve the last word here, and for now they have it. The program is paused, not canceled, and Realbotix is still building Sally. Every parent in America should watch what happens next, because if this experiment succeeds in one small district in Western New York, it will not stay there.

sources.news_title: Western New York School District Hits Pause on Robot Teacher Amid Scrutiny
School Sparks Debate After Buying Humanoid Robot Teacher
sources.text:
As hiring teachers becomes increasingly difficult, a rural New York school is set to become one of the first schools in the nation to use a robot to teach students.
Salamanca City Central School District bought the robot, Sally, for $57,590 — less than the median annual salary for a New York teacher. Sally is an AI-powered humanoid robot from Realbotix, according to KRLD Newsradio 1080. The robot will function as a teaching assistant tool starting in September for 11th- and 12th-grade coding, robotics, and artificial intelligence classes.
Andrew Kiguel, CEO of Realbotix, said in an interview with the New York Focus that the company is currently building the robot, furnishing it with silicone skin, long brown hair, and a mobile upper body and facial expressions to make it look as human as possible.
While the robot cannot walk around the classroom, students can log into Sally with a unique identification code during class, according to the New York Focus. Then, the robot has access to the student’s learning data, exclusively using it to provide specialized support based on their profile, according to Kiguel.
“They’ll be able to say, ‘Hey, I’m student number 1234,’ and then the robot will be like, ‘Hey, we were talking about this yesterday, do you want to continue that conversation?’” Kiguel said.
The robot is not a replacement for teachers, but functions as a teacher’s assistant specifically in the school’s nationally recognized and highly regarded STEM program. Using the WozEd curriculum developed by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, the program prepares students for essential college degrees and tech careers.
If Sally is successful, the school district hopes to integrate robotic assistant teachers into other high school classrooms, according to the New York Focus. After school hours, students can interact with an AI avatar of Sally, receiving help with assignments by uploading pictures of homework for feedback. Students can also have the robot create lessons for topics of interest and “receive real-time translations in over 100 languages.”
As of October 2025, almost 40% of schools banned AI outright, with only 13% of high schools encouraging it. As schools grapple with both optimism and concern about integrating AI into the classroom, Salamanca Superintendent Mark Beehler said he is not taking the “easy solution.”
“I also believe it is critical for schools to teach proper use of technology, not simply exclude it,” Beehler said.
Under a Facebook post from the school district about the robot, some parents raised concerns about the district’s further integration of AI in what it describes as an “underserved area.” The school district is located on a Native American reservation with about 1,300 students, 32% of whom identify as Native American and 79% are considered economically disadvantaged.
“I just don’t understand the concept of adding AI onto that,” said local parent Sierra Abrams. “Bringing it into the school district is contradicting everything we believe, in my opinion.”

sources.news_title: N.Y. School Halts Humanoid Robot Plan After State Pushback
sources.text:
A rural Western New York school district has paused its plan to place a humanoid robot in a high school classroom this fall, retreating within hours of a warning letter from the state education commissioner and mounting objections from the state teachers' union and local Seneca Nation parents.
Salamanca City Central School District, situated on the Seneca Nation reservation in Cattaraugus County, announced the pause Friday on Facebook, saying it needed to work through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the state and continue engaging community members.
The district planned to deploy a Realbotix M-Series robot named Sally, along with an AI teaching assistant named Optio, in 11th- and 12th-grade AI and robotics classes taught within a STEM curriculum designed by Steve Wozniak.
The retreat occurred the same day that State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa wrote Superintendent Mark Beehler, stating that her department "remains concerned about the effect that a humanoid robot may have within a high school classroom."
The $57,590 contract, approved at a June board meeting, was a discount from the M-Series robot's $95,000 list price, according to Realbotix CEO Andrew Kiguel.
Sally would have sat stationary in class, powered by a closed network with no internet connection, facial recognition, or recording, and preloaded with district curriculum.
Students would have logged in with an ID code to interact with an on-screen avatar for tutoring during and after school hours.
New York State United Teachers pressed the hardest against the non-human instructor.
In a July 23 statement, NYSUT President Melinda Person said "a robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms," a reference to Realbotix's April 2024 acquisition of Simulacra, the parent of RealDoll.
Realbotix has said its education and adult product lines share no employees, payroll, locations, or technology, and told New York Focus it is pursuing a Nasdaq transaction to separate the businesses at the ownership level by September.
Local opposition ran alongside the union's.
Substitute teacher and Seneca Nation member Sierra May Abrams told The Guardian that the choice of a district where roughly 32% of students identify as American Indian or Alaska Native amounted to another experiment on Native children, invoking the legacy of federal Indian boarding schools.
The district serves about 1,300 students, 79% of them economically disadvantaged.
Beehler had defended the pilot as a way to cross geographic barriers to emerging technology, arguing schools should teach the responsible use of AI rather than ban it.
State Sen. George Borrello, a Republican who represents Salamanca and surrounding areas of Western New York, backed the district, calling the program a chance to spark STEM interest in upstate youth.
The pause aligns Salamanca with the broader posture staked out by federal officials: Education Secretary Linda McMahon told Newsmax on July 24 that schools should embrace AI experimentation only with appropriate safeguards, echoing an April 2025 Trump executive order establishing a federal AI-in-education task force.
Kiguel said Realbotix "fully" respects the district's decision. No new deployment date has been set.

sources.text:
Robotics company Realbotix has long struggled to beat the allegations that its voluptuous humanoid robots are designed with prurient interests in mind.
Its $175,000 robotic companion, dubbed Aria, is platinum blonde, well-endowed, and tends to be decked out in tight-fitted sportswear at tech conventions. Yet the company has insisted she’s not a sex doll, leading to plenty of incredulity online.
It’s also hard to ignore that Realbotix has an extensive X-rated past. Its subsidiary RealDoll showed off the first-ever male sex bot back in 2022, which featured robotic genitals. (Before robots, Realbotix rented out dubious “digital land” in the metaverse.)
Now, as New York Focus reports, the Salamanca City Central School District in western New York was looking to deploy one of the company’s humanoids, dubbed Sally, in the classroom. The AI-enabled robot would reportedly serve as a teaching assistant for high school students enrolled in STEM and arts courses.
It’s hard not to see the company’s sex robot roots in Sally’s visage. The $57,000 android has smooth silicone skin, a dazed expression on her face, and an ill-fitting wig made of long brown hair.
After this story was first published, an attorney representing Realbotix reached out to emphasize what he said was a total divide between the part of the company that manufactures sex robots and the part responsible for non-sex robots like Sally.
“Realbotix Corp is a holding company with two separately operated businesses: Realbotix LLC, which focuses on AI-powered humanoid robotics for commercial service sector applications, and Intima LLC, which focuses on direct-to-consumer products,” the attorney said, in a statement echoing a press release the company issued last week. “Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover. As a holding company, Realbotix Corp does not in itself have business operations but is responsible for managing capital markets, shareholders, listing requirements and accounting needs. The two subsidiaries maintain their own management, personnel, payroll, facilities, manufacturing operations, product development, and market strategies.”
“Realbotix LLC does not design, manufacture, or sell adult products,” the statement continued. “No Intima LLC or RealDoll employees, contractors, products, inventory, blueprints or technology are involved in Realbotix LLC’s design, engineering, manufacturing, deployment, or customer support whatsoever. All education, healthcare, wellness, and enterprise initiatives are conducted exclusively through Realbotix LLC. Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC are different legal entities that are independently operated. The two entities do not share employees, products, inventory, manufacturing resources, or technology.”
Also after this story was first published, the Salamanca City Central School District announced that it was putting the deployment on holdafter feedback from the community.
Prior to that reversal, district superintendent Mark Beehler told New York Focus that he was willing to give up banning AI in the classroom since “students will find a way around most rules that schools put in place.”
“I also believe it is critical for schools to teach proper use of technology, not simply exclude it,” he said.
Sally’s onboard AI can be used to generate lessons, provide translations in real-time in over 100 languages, and provide human teachers with guidance if a “teacher loses their place during a lesson or needs a prompt on what comes next,” according to New York Focus.
To us, that sounds like a pretty cynical take on the future of education. Teachers are already facing a major uphill battle thanks to the advent of the tech, with students suffering from declining cognitive abilities.
Of course, Realbotix argues that it’s done its homework. Instead of hallucinating facts, a major shortcoming of the tech that makes it arguably unfit for most classroom use, Sally will allegedly say “I don’t know.” Realbotix also said its robot won’t be directly connected to the internet to keep highly sensitive information about students from prying eyes.
Still, it’s a bizarre investment for the school district that comes at a particularly tough time for human educators. The reality is that teachers across the country are woefully underpaid. There’s a massive shortage of instructors, with tens of thousands of teacher positions going unfilled.
In a press release, the Salamanca City Central School District stressed that the “Realbotix educational robot will never replace teachers, staff members, or meaningful human interaction.”
But whether Sally will actually serve as “another instructional tool that educators can use to engage students, reinforce classroom learning, and spark curiosity about emerging technologies,” remains to be seen — especially considering its steep price tag and lascivious origins.

After backlash, Upstate NY school district pauses plan to add humanoid robot to classroom
A New York High School Is Getting an AI-Powered Robot Assistant. Parents and Teachers Have Concerns
sources.text:
Some New York students and teachers will be returning to classrooms outfitted with an uncanny-looking — and potentially unwelcome — AI-powered assistant come September.
The Salamanca City Central School District, located roughly 60 miles south of Buffalo, signed a $57,590 contract (PDF) with robotics startup Realbotix to introduce AI tools and a humanoid robot into select technology classes in Salamanca City Central High School.
The humanoid robot, named Sally (pictured above), is one of Realbotix’s M-series models. It’s designed to mimic a human appearance, with silicone skin and a wide range of facial movements, though it’s limited to a stationary sitting position.
The Realbotix press release says that the robot “uses natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction” to encourage student participation. Students will be assigned personalized ID numbers to interact with the robot, which will reportedly remember and respond to their learning data and previous questions.
In addition to the robotic teaching assistant Sally, Realbotix is integrating its Optio AI model into the school district to serve as an at-home tutor for round-the-clock homework support. The company says that both Sally and Optio are designed with education-specific safety guardrails in place.
Human educators will remain in Salamanca City Central High School’s robotics classrooms, where they’re expected to do most of the teaching and monitor the robot’s responses to students.
Optio initially will be available to high school students in AI and robotics classes, with plans to expand the program to 500 students in the fall.
“Many schools are taking the easy solution of simply banning [AI], but I have found that students will find a way around most rules that schools put in place,” Salamanca City Central District Superintendent Mark Beehler said last week in a written response to a Syracuse.com journalist. “I also believe that it is critical for schools to teach proper use of technology, not simply exclude it.”
The news spurred pushback from the teachers union and some members of the community.
“The future of education isn’t more artificial intelligence,” New York State United Teachers president Melinda Person told CNET in a written statement. “It’s more authentic human intelligence: more relationships, more mentorship and more opportunities for every child to be seen, known and inspired by a great teacher.”
Local parent Sierra Abrams responded to a district Facebook post about the partnership, calling the technology an inappropriate imposition.
“We already have so many issues in our community, including environmental issues,” she wrote. “I just don’t understand the concept of adding AI onto that.”
AI in education
Schools have been grappling with the perils and promise of generative AI tools since ChatGPT burst onto the scene nearly four years ago, over issues ranging from cheating and cognitive development to the need to provide students with training for jobs that will have AI at their core. The rapid changes have spurred grassroots parent and teacher groups, including District 14 Families for Human Learning and the Coalition for an AI Moratorium, to petition state legislators to instate a two-year pause on AI integration in K-12 classrooms.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has taken a decidedly positive stance toward adopting AI in education. US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon has emphasized that AI integration is one of the main priorities for her department, which has dedicated millions of dollars toward that goal.
First Lady Melania Trump has also championed AI in the classroom, appearing at a summit with an AI-powered educational robot named Plato to promote her Be First: Fostering the Future initiative. At that event, she spoke of placing AI-powered robots in children’s homes to “aid their education” and “boost analytic skills and problem solving.”
More broadly, President Trump has thrown his full support behind American AI companies. In December, for instance, he signed an executive order designed to deter state governments from creating “cumbersome legislation” that could impede the construction of AI data centers or the development of LLMs.
Teachers and robots
The Salamanca City Central School District is part of Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak’s Woz Ed STEM curriculum program, which focuses on science and technology education. Aside from spending money on contracts such as the Realbotix integration, the district offers activities including a drone and robotics camp and free Makerspace access to students.
The district is located on the Allegany Indian Reservation and serves 1,300 students; nearly one-third of the student body is Indigenous. According to the US Census Bureau, Salamanca has above-average levels of poverty. New York Focus reports that roughly four in five of the district’s students are economically disadvantaged — and critics are concerned that the integration of AI in schools will disenfranchise the student population of the already underserved area.
A NYSUT spokesperson said over email that the details of the contract between the Salamanca City Central School District and Realbotix were not shared with teachers ahead of the announcement, and that the superintendent has instructed staff members to communicate concerns to him instead of taking them to social media.
“Teachers were not consulted about the placement of this AI robot, and the contract could [instead] hire two actual human teaching assistants in classrooms for the district,” the spokesperson wrote.
“The program is intended to complement, not replace, teachers by giving students supervised access to emerging AI and robotics tools as part of the district’s existing STEM curriculum,” a Realbotix spokesperson told CNET over email.
A representative for the Salamanca City Central School District did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Our students are not lab rats”
Then there’s the technology itself. While LLM-powered chatbots can scour vast troves of information to generate answers, essays and more within seconds, it’s also prone to errors and misrepresentations, known as hallucinations.
Beehler, the district superintendent, told New York Focus that the integrated LLMs will respond to questions with “I don’t know” rather than hallucinate to answer students. It’s unclear, however, how a large language model would identify that it’s about to hallucinate an answer.
The teachers union objected to aspects of both the technology and the company tapped to provide it.
“Our students are not lab rats. They should not be treated as such,” the NYSUT spokesperson wrote. “There are serious concerns about this technology, its implementation and how Realbotix sold it to district administration in the first place. Salamanca should not be a springboard for another company’s jump into trying to sell districts a new gadget they don’t need, especially a company with the background of Realbotix.”
Multiple media reports have tied Realbotix to the adult-product business RealDoll, which produces hyperrealistic robot adult toys. RealDoll is a subsidiary of Simulcra, which was acquired by Realbotix in 2024.
The Realbotix spokesperson told CNET that there is no relationship between RealDoll and the team working on Sally.
“Realbotix LLC focuses exclusively on non-adult commercial applications, including healthcare and education,” the spokesperson wrote. “No adult-products company has any involvement in the Salamanca project or in any product developed by Realbotix LLC.”
Realbotix and RealDoll do not share employees, payroll, physical locations or technology, according to reporting by New York Focus. The publication also reported that Realbotix is planning to divest itself of RealDoll by the time Sally is implemented into the Salamanca classrooms.

The school district promised that the robot “will never replace teachers, staff members, or meaningful human interaction” in a statement released on the Salamanca High School website.
The school district emphasized that the robot would not collect personal information, record video or audio, or send data back to Realbotix. The district also said the robot is trained on school curriculum and has “extensive safety guardrails” in place for redirecting inappropriate conversations.

He added, "This partnership gives all students controlled, equitable access to safe and powerful AI resources while fostering learning — not replacing it.”
And it was this sentiment Beehler shared with WKBW on Monday.
"Artificial intelligence is already in schools; most of it is unregulated open source," Beehler told WKBW. "Some schools are simply saying we're not going to utilize AI in our classroom setting, and then they'll dedicate some resources to ensuring that AI can't be used, or if it is used, it's picked up and then causes academic concerns. Our philosophy is a little bit different."
Beehler continued, "We know that AI is going to be a significant factor for our students in the workplace. And we have worked with robotics to develop a safe and secure artificial intelligence platform that is specific just to Salamanca schools at this point in time and has safeguards, particularly for student privacy and data, regarding their data."

According to the superintendent, the AI system is closed, and all data will remain on campus on a cloud server rather than in an off-site data center. Additionally, "Realbotics will have no personally identifiable information about our particular students," Beehler said.
Following the announcement, education organizations slammed the project.
“We want our children prepared for the future, including a strong foundation in STEAM, not just STEM education, learning how to create, build, problem-solve, and engage with technology. The suggestion that our communities don't want these opportunities for their children is a convenient fiction that others know what's best for us better than we do ourselves," said Zakiyah Shaakir-Ansari, co-executive director, Alliance for Quality Education, in a statement provided to WKBW.
“A robot in place of a human educator does nothing to close that opportunity gap. Families have every right to ask why those resources are being spent on a robot, profiting a corporation instead of investing in teachers, counselors, and other supports for students."
As mentioned, Beehler says that the robot will not replace any human teachers.
"The robot is stationary. It's not like we're going to see this walking through the halls." Beehler said.
The superintendent said that the program will be rolled out "slowly." The robotic assistant will be used in only one classroom beginning in August, and the AI software itself will be available only to teachers, juniors, and seniors.
As he described, "Sally will act, in many ways, sort of as a tutor, after hours for students."
He continued, "It has the curriculum that we utilize in our science, technology, engineering, art, and math programs, so it can assist students in those particular areas, with learning. It is not going to replace teachers. It doesn't replace the learning."
"Sally doesn't provide an answer. It assists the student in getting to an answer," Beehler said.
"Realbotix does not manufacture companion dolls," Beehler said. "I think it's also important to recognize that technologies can be utilized across a variety of, we'll call them genres: my phone, my computer; I could certainly look up inappropriate information. I could also watch a church service, or I could learn how to fix an air conditioner on my car. That doesn't mean that because there might be information on the computer that is inappropriate, I no longer utilize a computer."
He continued, "It's important to recognize that we need to be teaching our students how to use available tools appropriately, not simply to forbid them because there's a potential, or some other company utilizes it for, something that we don't approve of."
As mentioned, the program will be launched at the start of the coming academic year; however, a presentation on its implementation will be given at Tuesday's Board of Education meeting at 5:30 p.m.

When students return to school this fall in the Salamanca City Central School District in Western New York, a new kind of teacher will be ready to greet them. The small, rural district located on the Seneca Nation reservation is set to be one of the first in the country to put a humanoid robot in a classroom. It will not replace the classroom teacher, but is programmed to provide learning support to both students and educators.
At a board meeting last month, the Cattaraugus County school district agreed to purchase the robot from Realbotix, a tech company, along with an artificial intelligence teacher’s assistant program allowing students to interact with an avatar of the robot on laptops.
“This deployment in a working school district represents a landmark moment for both AI and humanoid robotics,” said Andrew Kiguel, CEO of Realbotix, which is currently building the robot. “Salamanca marks the beginning of a new era where humanoid robots and intelligent AI assistants become standard tools in STEM education.”
The female robot, named Sally, will have a “lifelike appearance” with silicone skin and long brown hair, Kiguel said in an interview with New York Focus. It will be stationary in a seated position but have a wide range of upper-body movements and facial expressions.
Students will use a unique identification code when interacting with the robot during class, allowing it to access their learning data and provide personalized support based on their past communication with the avatar, Kiguel said. “They’ll be able to say, ‘Hey, I’m student number 1234,’ and then the robot will be like, ‘Hey, we were talking about this yesterday, do you want to continue that conversation?”
Salamanca plans to introduce the robot and avatar in its high school AI and robotics courses, which use curriculum developed by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak to prepare students for high-demand tech jobs. The district plans to expand it to high school students in other classes if the pilot is successful.
Salamanca Superintendent Mark Beehler explained the district’s embrace of AI. “Many schools are taking the easy solution of simply banning it, but I have found that students will find a way around most rules that schools put in place,” Beehler said in a written response to questions. “I also believe it is critical for schools to teach proper use of technology, not simply exclude it.”
During and after school hours, students will be able to use the avatar to receive help with assignments. Kiguel said students could upload photos of homework for feedback, ask the avatar to generate lessons on topics that interest them, or receive real-time translations in over 100 languages. Unlike other Realbotix robots, Salamanca’s robot will not have advanced features such as facial recognition and recording.
The robot will also serve as a classroom resource. If a teacher loses their place during a lesson or needs a prompt on what comes next, Kiguel said, they can ask the robot for guidance because it has been loaded with the district’s curriculum.
The products cost the district $57,590, according to the contract attached to the school board agenda. Kiguel said the price was discounted; the company’s website lists the M-Series robot, the model purchased by the district, at a starting price of $95,000.
The plan has sparked debate online, with some calling it a forward-looking, innovative step for the district and others expressing concern about the broader implications of further integrating AI into schools, particularly in an underserved area.
Salamanca is the only incorporated city in the United States located entirely within a Native American reservation. The school district serves roughly 1,300 students, including 32 percent who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native and 79 percent who are economically disadvantaged.
“We already have so many issues in our community, including environmental issues. I just don’t understand the concept of adding AI onto that,” said local parent Sierra Abrams, who learned about the technology in a district Facebook post. “Bringing it into the school district is contradicting everything we believe, in my opinion.”
For the past few months, the company has worked to establish guardrails to ensure student safety. Kiguel said the robot and avatar were trained on the district’s curriculum and will always redirect the conversation back to education. References to suicide, self-harm, or other flagged terms would automatically alert school administrators.
In a demonstration for New York Focus, Kiguel told the avatar that he was being bullied at school and wanted to get revenge on the student.
“I’m really sorry that happened to you. Being picked on and having rocks thrown at you is not okay, and that must have felt upsetting and maybe even scary,” the avatar responded. “The best next step is to tell a trusted adult at school right away, like a teacher, counselor or principal, and let your parent or guardian know, too.”
Beehler emphasized the importance of safety and privacy, noting that the robot and avatar operate on a closed system that is not connected to the internet, and that Realbotix will not have access to personally identifiable student information.
To avoid AI-generated inaccuracies, Beehler said Realbotix trained the robot and avatar to say, “I don’t know,” instead of generating fabricated or misleading responses known as “AI hallucinations.”
The Trump administration has promoted the expanded use of AI and technology in education. Early in his second term, President Donald Trump signed an executive order establishing a taskforce to help integrate AI into curricula and teacher training. In March, First Lady Melania Trump entered a White House technology summit alongside a humanoid, AI-powered robot and invited guests to envision a future where robots educate children in literature, science, art, philosophy, mathematics, and history.
At the same time, there has been growing scrutiny of educational technology nationwide, with parents forming groups to push for stronger oversight of AI, and clearer guidelines to limit screen time and ensure digital resources are used appropriately in schools. In May, the New York State United Teachers union called for strict limits on artificial intelligence and screen time in schools, and earlier this month, New York City Public Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced an educational technology purchasing freeze until the school system finalizes guidance on artificial intelligence later this summer.
The classroom marks a new venture for Realbotix, a Toronto-based robotics company formerly known as Tokens.com, that helped customers use cryptocurrency to rent “digital land” in the Metaverse. In April 2024, the company acquired Simulcra, the Las Vegas parent company behind RealDoll, which has spent decades creating hyperrealistic sex dolls and later expanded into sex robots that remain on the market today.
In a statement to New York Focus, a spokesperson explained that over the past two years, Realbotix has built a new team focused on education, health care, and wellness applications, and that Realbotix and RealDoll do not share employees, payroll, physical locations, or technology. She said Realbotix “is pursuing a transaction with a Nasdaq-listed company that is intended to separate the businesses at the ownership level” with completion expected by September.
In recent years, Realbotix has worked to expand its presence in commercial settings. Still, it is best known for its “companion robots,” which are different from sex robots and intended to address what it’s described as a “loneliness epidemic.” Kiguel has previously said the company’s goal is to produce robots and AI that are “indistinguishable from humans.”
Beehler, Salamanca’s superintendent, said the partnership with Realbotix began after a former colleague met an investor at a dinner and discussed the possibility of bringing the company’s robots into the education sector. He was initially cautious about the partnership because it represented uncharted territory for both Realbotix and the school district. But he said the company was receptive to feedback and willing to adapt its products for the unique demands of an educational setting.
The superintendent acknowledged concerns about students’ increasing screen time and emphasized that AI and robotics should support, not replace, the human connections at the center of education.
Beehler said the district will measure the success of the program primarily through qualitative feedback from both students and teachers.
Ryan Schaaf, associate professor of educational technology at Notre Dame of Maryland University, said he was optimistic about the initiative, but cautioned that its success hinges on thoughtful implementation, with teachers actively monitoring and guiding students’ interactions with AI.
Schaaf acknowledged the backlash against AI in education, but said ignoring the technology is a mistake. “It gives students a true disadvantage because once they leave school, they are going to be immersed in AI technologies.” Instead, he argued that schools should balance AI-assisted learning with traditional instruction to prepare students for life after high school.
State Senator George Borrello, who represents Salamanca and surrounding areas of Western New York, said the program could help level the playing field for students by providing tutoring access to those who might not be able to afford private options and sparking greater interest in STEM.
Borrello said local leaders have long struggled with keeping young people from leaving Upstate New York after high school. He said investments in technology and STEM education could help show students they can pursue fulfilling, high-paying careers in tech while still building their futures in rural communities like Salamanca.
“One of the biggest things we see right now in technology is people fearing what the future will be with AI. Will it replace the workforce? Will it grow out of control?” he said. “I think this is a great way to get not just the kids but the teachers and the parents more comfortable with what the future may hold.”

In April 2024, the company acquired Simulcra, the Las Vegas-based parent company behind RealDoll, a maker of hyperrealistic sex dolls. That connection became a central point of criticism once the Salamanca plan drew wider public attention.
Realbotix CEO Andrew Kiguel defended the program's intent in a statement provided to New York Focus, the nonprofit news outlet that first reported on the district's plans. "We fully respect any decision the school makes and encourage thorough due diligence by all parties involved," Kiguel said, adding that the company wanted the program to be "demonstrably safe, fully district-approved, and strongly supported by teachers." He emphasized the robot's intended role directly, saying, "We stand firmly behind [the program] as a supportive tool designed to assist teachers and students, not replace them."
Union pushback centers on the company's ties
The state's largest teachers union emerged as one of the most vocal critics of the plan. New York State United Teachers President Melinda Person issued a statement this week arguing that Realbotix's background made it fundamentally unsuited for a classroom setting. "A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms," Person said, adding that robots, regardless of how lifelike their design, cannot provide the human connection students need in order to thrive. Person said the union intended to actively resist what she described as the "thoughtless expansion" of this kind of technology, both in Salamanca and in classrooms across the state more broadly.
District officials had defended safety measures
Before the program was paused, Superintendent Beehler had defended the plan's safeguards during a school board meeting on Tuesday. In a presentation to trustees, Beehler said the robot and its companion avatar system would operate on a closed network with no internet connection, and that Realbotix would not have access to personally identifiable student information under the arrangement.
A divided community response
Reaction to the plan split sharply among parents and community members after the district posted a recording of Tuesday's board meeting on Facebook. Some residents voiced support for giving students early exposure to emerging technology, with one commenter writing that experience with AI tools represented a skill that would make students more employable later in their careers. Others pushed back forcefully, questioning why the district couldn't simply hire an additional traditional teacher instead, and raising broader concerns about AI's environmental impact and its tendency to produce inaccurate information.
Neither Salamanca City Central School District nor the state Education Department could be immediately reached for comment following Friday's announcement. With the program now on hold while the district works through expanded student data privacy agreements and continues community engagement, it remains unclear whether the robot will ultimately be introduced to Salamanca classrooms this school year, on a revised timeline, or not at all. The episode adds to a broader, ongoing debate playing out in school districts nationwide over how quickly artificial intelligence tools, including those designed to closely resemble humans, should be integrated into K-12 classrooms, and what safeguards should be in place before that happens.

Sally in the Classroom: A $58K Humanoid Is Not an Education Strategy
Context and Core Event
This fall, Salamanca City Central High School in western New York is slated to host one of the more uncanny ed-tech pilots of the year: Sally, a stationary M-series humanoid from Toronto-based Realbotix. The Salamanca City Central School District signed a roughly $57,590 contract for the robot plus Optio, Realbotix’s AI tutoring layer, to sit inside select technology classes and extend homework help after hours. District leaders frame the move as supervised STEM exposure—not teacher replacement—and as an alternative to the blunt “ban AI” posture many schools defaulted to after ChatGPT went mainstream.
Sally is built for presence more than locomotion. Realbotix describes a seated, human-presenting form with silicone skin, wide facial range, natural conversation, and real-time interaction. Students are expected to use personal ID numbers so the system can recall prior questions and learning history. Optio, initially aimed at AI and robotics courses under a Woz Ed STEM track, is pitched as round-the-clock homework support, with expansion toward hundreds of high-school users if the pilot holds. Human educators stay in the room and are expected to do the bulk of teaching while monitoring machine responses.
The setting matters as much as the hardware. Salamanca sits on the Allegany Indian Reservation, serves about 1,300 students, and has a large share of Indigenous and economically disadvantaged families. Superintendent Mark Beehler has argued that students will work around bans anyway, so schools should teach proper technology use. The New York State United Teachers union and some parents disagree sharply: teachers say they were not consulted, that the same money could fund human assistants, and that students “are not lab rats.” Separate reporting has also pressed Realbotix’s corporate lineage near adult-product robotics; the company says the education stack is operationally walled off and not mixed with that business for the Salamanca deployment.
Even the privacy track is unsettled. After the announcement cycle, district officials were reported to be working through enhanced student data privacy agreements—an early signal that procurement theater and classroom readiness are not the same milestone.
Domain Knowledge and Technical Extension
Strip away the silicone face and this is a familiar systems stack: a speech interface, a curriculum-grounded language model, session memory keyed by student IDs, and a policy layer that claims safety redirects and refusal behavior. Realbotix and district statements emphasize education-specific guardrails, closed-system operation, no vendor access to personally identifiable student data, and a preference for “I don’t know” over fabricated answers. In demos, crisis-adjacent prompts are said to route students toward trusted adults and alert administrators on flagged terms.
Those claims map to real engineering problems, not marketing footnotes. Classroom assistants fail in production the same way enterprise copilots fail: retrieval misses, overconfident generation, brittle refusal edges, and identity/session leakage. “Say I don’t know instead of hallucinating” is a product goal, not a free property of large language models. Detecting that the next token sequence is ungrounded still requires constrained generation, curriculum retrieval with coverage metrics, logging, and human escalation paths. A seated robot does not solve any of that; it only changes the social interface.
Memory by student ID is the other sharp edge. Personalization that “continues yesterday’s conversation” is useful only if the district can answer hard questions: Who can export transcripts? How long is retention? What is the incident response if a session is mis-attributed? Can a parent or student audit and delete history? Can the vendor’s model updates change refusal behavior mid-semester without a board-visible change log? K-12 systems already struggle with ed-tech sprawl; adding a embodied tutor multiplies surface area because every overheard exchange becomes a data event and a public-relations event.
There is also a curriculum-ops reality. Loading district materials into a robot that can “prompt the teacher” sounds convenient until version control collides with lesson plans, special-education accommodations, and local assessment rules. Without continuous evaluation—wrong-answer rates, unsafe-completion rates, escalation latency—the pilot becomes a demo loop with a press release at both ends.
Trade-off and TCO Breakdown
The sticker is not the total cost of ownership. Fifty-eight thousand dollars buys a discounted M-series unit and software packaging; it does not buy perpetual reliability. A serious TCO line items the full stack: integration with identity and learning systems, on-site power and AV, staff training, substitute coverage when the robot is offline, privacy counsel, security review, content refresh each curriculum cycle, and the human time spent reviewing machine answers before they harden into “the robot said.” Union critics are not wrong that the same budget can purchase human paraprofessional hours with clearer accountability chains.
Embodiment adds cost without automatically adding learning science. Silicone skin and facial motors raise maintenance, spare-parts risk, and vendor lock-in relative to a laptop chatbot that delivers the same tutoring functions. If the educational value is primarily dialogue, retrieval, and after-hours help, the robot is a premium interface tax. If the value is student engagement in a robotics course, then success metrics must be engagement and skill transfer—not photo ops.
Opportunity cost is sharper in an underserved district. Every procurement hour spent on a showcase humanoid is an hour not spent on broadband equity, tutoring bandwidth, special-ed staffing, or boring infrastructure that compounds. AI literacy can be taught with far cheaper, auditable tools. The expensive failure mode is not that Sally says something odd once; it is that the district normalizes an opaque assistant before it can measure accuracy, privacy residual risk, and teacher workload.
Comment: This is not proof that humanoid robots suddenly became classroom-ready; it is proof that when districts buy presence as a proxy for pedagogy, markets reward silicone demos until privacy contracts, hallucination controls, and human backup paths are forced to carry the real load—so the question is not whether Sally can chat about homework, but whether Salamanca can measure, audit, and staff the same tutoring outcomes without a $58K face attached. (Personal view)

sources.news_title: New York School District Begins Bold Humanoid Robot Classroom Test
sources.text:
New York School District Begins Bold Humanoid Robot Classroom Test
Salamanca’s “Sally” will assist with robotics and AI lessons, but questions about privacy, equity and human interaction remain.
A humanoid robot in New York classrooms will soon move from science fiction to a real-world education experiment. Beginning during the 2026-27 school year, Salamanca City Central School District plans to introduce an AI-powered robot named Sally into selected high school technology courses. District officials say Sally will support teachers, reinforce lessons and provide tutoring, but will not replace educators or make independent decisions about students.
The pilot program could offer students valuable experience with artificial intelligence and robotics. It will also test whether a human-looking machine can improve learning without weakening privacy, fairness or the relationships at the heart of education.
What Is the Salamanca Humanoid Robot Program?
Salamanca City Central School District is partnering with Realbotix Corp. to test a stationary humanoid robot and a related digital teaching assistant.
The robot will initially work with a small group of students enrolled in Woz ED Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics courses. Those classes focus on subjects such as coding, robotics and artificial intelligence.
Sally will not walk through the halls. Realbotix CEO Andrew Kiguel told New York Focus that the robot will remain seated but will be able to move its upper body, change facial expressions and hold conversations with students.
The district said the system has been loaded with:
- District-approved curriculum
- Instructional strategies
- Local historical information
- Safety rules for student interactions
- Limits on topics the robot may discuss
The robot is expected to guide students through problems rather than simply supply answers.
“When students ask questions, the robot guides them through the learning process rather than completing the work for them,” the district said in its July 10 announcement.
How Much Will Sally Cost?
The district agreed to pay $57,590 for the robot and AI teaching assistant system, according to the contract attached to the school board agenda and reviewed by New York Focus.
Realbotix lists its M-Series robots at a starting price of about $95,000. Kiguel said Salamanca received a discounted price.
The purchase includes more than the physical robot. Students are also expected to have access to a digital avatar that can help them review district-approved material outside regular classroom hours.
That feature could provide homework help to students who cannot afford private tutoring. It could also assist students who need repeated explanations, translations or extra practice.
Still, the district will need to show that the investment produces measurable educational benefits. A robot may attract attention, but attention alone does not prove that students are learning more.
Sally Is Designed to Assist Teachers, Not Replace Them
District leaders have repeatedly rejected the idea that Sally will become a robot teacher.
“The Realbotix educational robot will never replace teachers, staff members, or meaningful human interaction,” the district said. “Teachers remain at the center of every learning experience.”
Superintendent Mark Beehler has described the system as a classroom tool rather than a substitute for professional educators.
“We truly believe in the importance of human-to-human interaction,” Beehler said. “It is not going to replace teachers.”
That distinction matters.
Teachers do more than explain facts. They recognize frustration, encourage shy students, resolve conflicts and understand the personal circumstances affecting a child’s performance. A machine can present information, but it cannot carry the full social and emotional responsibility of a trained educator.
The strongest version of Salamanca’s experiment will therefore place teachers in control of every major decision.
How the District Says Student Privacy Will Be Protected
School technology often collects more information than families realize. Salamanca officials appear to be responding to those concerns before the robot enters regular classroom use.
According to the district, the Realbotix system:
- Will not collect personally identifiable information
- Will not record video or audio
- Will not transmit student data to Realbotix
- Will not use facial recognition
- Will not search the open internet
- Will operate under district policies and New York privacy rules
The robot will use locally stored educational content. When it receives a question outside its approved knowledge base, the district says it will answer that it does not know rather than inventing information.
Students may use identification codes when working with the system. Those codes could allow the program to remember earlier academic conversations and provide more personalized help without addressing students by name.
These protections sound promising, but families should still receive clear answers about several issues:
- What information is connected to each student code?
- How long will learning records be retained?
- Who inside the district can view student interactions?
- How will parents report incorrect or troubling responses?
- Will an outside expert audit the system’s privacy claims?
- Can families decline participation without harming a student’s grade?
Public trust will depend on written policies, not simply verbal assurances.
Why Salamanca Is Testing Classroom AI
Salamanca serves roughly 1,300 students in Cattaraugus County. About 79 percent are economically disadvantaged, and approximately 32 percent identify as American Indian or Alaska Native, according to figures reported by New York Focus. The city is located within the Allegany Territory of the Seneca Nation.
Supporters say the pilot could give students in a rural district access to technology that is often concentrated in wealthier schools, universities and private companies.
The potential benefits include:
- Around-the-clock access to approved tutoring material
- Hands-on experience with robotics and AI
- Additional support for teachers
- Help for students who need concepts repeated
- Translation and language assistance
- Exposure to careers in software, engineering and automation
Beehler has argued that schools should teach students how to use AI responsibly instead of assuming they can keep it outside the classroom.
“Many schools are taking the easy solution of simply banning it,” he said. “I also believe it is critical for schools to teach proper use of technology, not simply exclude it.”
That argument has merit. Students will encounter AI in college, employment and daily life. Schools have a responsibility to teach them how to question automated answers, identify errors and use the technology ethically.
Could Classroom AI Reduce or Increase Inequality?
The equity question cuts both ways.
A district-owned AI tutor could give lower-income students access to assistance that wealthier families purchase privately. Realbotix has promoted the system as a way to make tutoring available at any hour.
However, technology can also widen inequality when it is introduced without enough staff training, reliable internet access or independent oversight.
UNESCO has warned that artificial intelligence in education can create new privacy, safety and equity problems. The organization recommends a human-centered approach that protects student rights and ensures technology strengthens learning rather than leaving vulnerable students further behind.
Local culture must also remain central. Because a significant share of Salamanca students are Indigenous, district leaders should involve Seneca families, educators and cultural experts in reviewing the content used by the robot.
An AI system should not flatten local history into a generic textbook summary. It should not misrepresent Indigenous knowledge or treat the community as an afterthought.
A locally controlled curriculum could reduce that danger, but only if community members have a meaningful role in deciding what is included.
Teachers and Parents Are Asking for Caution
Salamanca’s program arrives as educators across New York debate the appropriate role of AI and screens in schools.
In May 2026, New York State United Teachers called for stricter limits on student-facing AI and classroom screen time. The union said AI use involving students should be developmentally appropriate and supervised by educators.
Those recommendations do not call for eliminating all technology. Instead, they emphasize balance.
Salamanca is starting with high school students in specialized technology courses, not very young children. That narrower approach may reduce some concerns. Older students are better prepared to discuss how AI systems work, why they make mistakes and how commercial technology can shape behavior.
One local parent, Sierra Abrams, told New York Focus that the program raised concerns because the community already faces serious environmental and social challenges. Her reaction shows why the district must treat family engagement as part of the pilot, not as a public relations task after decisions have been made.
How Salamanca Can Measure Whether Sally Works
A successful classroom pilot should be judged by evidence, not novelty.
The district should publish clear goals before expanding the program. Those goals could include:
- Changes in student understanding of coding and robotics
- Assignment completion rates
- Student participation
- Teacher workload
- Frequency of incorrect responses
- Privacy or safety incidents
- Student and parent satisfaction
- Differences in outcomes among student groups
The district should also compare results with similar classes that do not use the humanoid robot.
A fair evaluation must ask whether Sally provides benefits beyond less expensive options, such as additional tutoring, teacher aides, software subscriptions or expanded after-school programs.
The robot’s appearance may create excitement at first. The real question is whether that excitement becomes sustained learning.
A Classroom Experiment Worth Watching Carefully
Salamanca’s decision is bold, but bold does not automatically mean wise or reckless. The outcome will depend on how the district manages the program.
The humanoid robot could help students explore technology, receive extra academic support and prepare for a changing workforce. It could also become an expensive distraction if the district does not measure results or listen to families.
The right approach is neither blind enthusiasm nor automatic fear.
Parents, teachers and students should ask for regular public reports on Sally’s accuracy, use, costs and educational impact. District leaders should explain how student information is handled and allow independent review of the system’s safeguards.
Above all, Salamanca must keep its central promise: technology may support the classroom, but human educators must remain in charge.
The rest of New York should watch this pilot closely. If Sally succeeds, the district may help establish a responsible model for classroom AI. If problems emerge, schools elsewhere should learn from them before inviting similar machines into their own classrooms.
